title: A Prospective Evaluation of LLM-Assisted Clinical Reporting and Information Extraction in Cardiology
summary: Writing discharge letters takes a lot of time for doctors. In addition, these letters are not always complete or easy to understand. This study examines whether a computer-based language program can meaningfully support doctors in writing discharge letters. The program will create a first draft of the letter based on the data already available in the medical record. This draft is then always reviewed, corrected, and signed by a doctor. The study is carried out on the cardiology wards of the University Medical Center Göttingen. Adult patients who underwent treatment of cardiac arrhythmias, heart valve treatment, or coronary artery treatment after a heart attack during their hospital stay can participate. The study compares the time required to write the letter, the quality of the letter, and the satisfaction of the medical staff between letters with and without computer support. No additional examinations or risks arise for the participating persons. Only data from the medical record that is already available will be used.
conditions: Patients after pulmonary vein isolation (PVI), transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) or acute percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) for myocardial infarction; the focus of the study is medical documentation (discharge letter creation), not the underlying disease.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
- Adult patients (≥ 18 years), capable of consent, hospitalized at one of the cardiology wards (2022, 5021, 5022, 1025) of the University Medical Center Göttingen.
- Pulmonary vein isolation (PVI), transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) or acute percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) for myocardial infarction performed during the current inpatient stay.
- Written informed consent.
Exclusion criteria:
- Minors (< 18 years).
- Patients lacking capacity to consent without an available legal representative or authorized proxy.
- Patients who refuse or withdraw their consent.
- Patients for whom adequate informed consent cannot be obtained despite supportive measures (e.g., interpreters, relatives, digital tools).
